opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being honest about both what we showed and what we didn't.

What I'm most excited about with that release is that it was the first time we had a single model doing a pretty broad range of dexterous tasks: folding laundry, bussing a table, assembling a box, packing items. And it wasn't a separate specialist policy for each one. It's one generalist model, pretrained on a large and diverse mixture of data from a bunch of different robot platforms, and then in some cases fine-tuned for the harder, longer-horizon tasks. Laundry folding in particular is something I'd wanted to see robots do well for a long time. Deformable objects, lots of variation in how a shirt lands in a pile, the need to recover when something goes wrong. Seeing the model handle that, and retry when a fold didn't go right, felt like a real step.

In terms of generalization, I'd say we saw meaningful generalization to new object instances and new configurations: different clothes, different items on the table, things it hadn't seen in exactly that arrangement. We also saw that pretraining on the broad mixture really helped compared to training from scratch on the target task. That's an important signal, because it suggests the data from other robots and other tasks is actually transferring.

But I don't want to overclaim. Most of those evaluations were in environments that weren't hugely different from the ones we collected data in. We weren't dropping the robot into a random home it had never seen and asking it to do whatever you said. Generalizing to entirely new environments, new tasks described in language, and really open-ended settings is still the frontier. A lot of what we've been focused on since then is exactly that: how do you get the model to work in places it's never been, and follow instructions for things it wasn't explicitly trained on?

So my overall assessment is that it showed the recipe works. Large, diverse data plus a big pretrained model gets you dexterity and some robustness you didn't really see before. But I'd say we're still early on the kind of broad, open-world generalization that people ultimately want from robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'd say I try to be pretty measured about it, because I think "generalization" gets used to mean a lot of different things in robotics, and it's worth being precise about what we actually saw.

The thing I'm most excited about is that the model is handling variation it never saw during training in a way that feels qualitatively different from what we had even a year or two ago. So it's not just, you know, we trained on a thousand episodes of folding this particular shirt in this particular lab, and it folds that shirt again. It's new objects, new initial configurations, scenes that are genuinely messier than anything in the data, and the policy recovers and keeps going. The laundry and the bussing-a-table style tasks are nice because they expose the long tail really quickly. The shirt crumples in a way you've never seen, something slips, and you find out pretty fast whether you've got a model that understands the task or one that's memorized a trajectory.

What I think is actually driving it is less any single architectural trick and more the recipe: pre-training on a large, diverse set of data across many robots and many tasks, and then post-training on higher-quality data for the specific behaviors you care about. Having a vision-language backbone that already has a lot of knowledge about objects and semantics helps a ton. And then the data diversity is doing a lot of the work. When we ablate and train only on the narrow task data, you lose most of the robustness, so the broad pre-training is clearly where the generalization is coming from.

Now, the caveats. I would not describe this as a robot that you can drop into an arbitrary home and have it work. The generalization we're seeing is within a distribution that's wider than before, but it's still a distribution. New homes, really different lighting, objects that are far outside anything in the data, long multi-step tasks where errors compound — those are all still hard, and the failure rates are higher than the demo videos would suggest. I always encourage people to look at the success rates and the number of attempts, not just the highlight reel.

So my honest assessment is that it's a real step. It's evidence that the scaling recipe that worked in language and vision is starting to work for robot control, and that was not obvious a couple years ago. But we're at the early part of that curve. The gap between "works impressively in a range of settings" and "works reliably everywhere" is where most of the remaining work is, and a lot of that comes down to data: more of it, more diverse, and better ways of using it.

astra-6.text:
I think the encouraging thing is that we’re seeing one model do a fairly broad range of tasks across different robots and environments. But generalization is a spectrum. Being able to handle a new object or a different arrangement of a scene is different from being able to do an entirely new task, and a successful demonstration doesn’t necessarily tell you which of those you’re seeing.

The questions I’d ask are: What was in the training data? How different is the test environment? And how reliably does it work across repeated attempts? Those distinctions matter a lot in robotics, because you can have a system that looks very capable and still needs substantial data for each new setting.

So I’d view the release as an encouraging step toward broader robot capabilities, while being careful about concluding that we’ve solved generalization. The really interesting test is what happens when you take the system into a new home, with unfamiliar objects, and ask it to do something without collecting a lot of additional data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what we mean by generalization. A robot doing a task in a new kitchen, with different objects and a different layout, is demonstrating something meaningful. But that’s different from being able to do an entirely new task, or handle any situation you might encounter in a home.

With a release like this, I’d want to understand what was in the training data, how different the evaluation settings were, and how consistently the robot succeeded across attempts. A video can show that a behavior is possible; it doesn’t tell you how reliable it is.

So I’d separate generalization to new objects and environments from generalization to new skills. Both are important, but evidence for one doesn’t automatically establish the other.
